strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets (vision and language) with extensive baselines (~30 methods across different categories)

weaknesses: Limited novelty: core idea of embedding regularization to suppress spurious features is not new; resembles recent work (ElRep, Hermann & Lampinen 2020); contribution is primarily incremental formulation

Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes binary classification, Gaussian distributions, extreme spurious correlations, and balanced priors. These rarely hold for deep networks on real data. The paper acknowledges but does not formally justify why regularization works for deep networks that violate assumptions

Marginal empirical improvements lacking statistical significance: improvements on most benchmarks are 0.7-1.0% (often within standard deviation ranges); no significance testing provided. E.g., Waterbirds: 91.2% vs 91.0% (DFR), CelebA: 91.4% vs 91.4% (ElRep/PDE), ColorMNIST: 73.6% vs 72.9% (PDE)

Weak connection between restrictive theoretical assumptions and practical algorithm: no validation that experimental datasets satisfy Gaussian assumption, constant core/spurious directions, or other theoretical requirements

Incomplete analysis: no ablation on direction aggregation strategy; no discussion of failure modes; limited exploration of method without group labels; missing comparison with causal debiasing literature
Presentation issues: figures cluttered, critical details relegated to appendices, theory-practice connection unclear, code URL missing, reproducibility concerns

strengths: Clear and insightful theoretical decomposition of worst-group error into spurious and core components (Theorem 1), providing principled motivation for the regularization approach

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 datasets with consistent improvements in worst-group accuracy; includes challenging scenarios (missing groups, noisy environment labels) demonstrating robustness
Practical and modular design that integrates with existing frameworks (EIIL) without requiring additional group annotations; shows effectiveness even with imperfect environment information

Strong qualitative analysis with t-SNE and Grad-CAM visualizations that provide convincing evidence the method learns domain-invariant representations aligned with labels rather than spurious attributes
Thorough experimental protocol with 18+ baselines across multiple robustness categories and extensive ablations (Tables 6, 18) validating design choices

weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 assumes Gaussian embeddings, extreme spurious correlations (P(y,d)≈0), linear classifiers, and binary/2-domain settings, but is applied to deep networks with multi-class/multi-domain problems; the claim that Gaussian assumptions are 'empirically well-grounded' provides insufficient justification

Method novelty is incremental: GroupDRO already addresses worst-group robustness; SCER primarily adds straightforward embedding regularization (products of alignment and magnitude terms). The specific loss formulation design choices lack deep justification beyond the limited theory

Empirical improvements are often marginal: CelebA (91.4% vs 91.0%), MetaShift (86.7% vs 85.6%) improvements fall within or near standard deviations; practical significance unclear. Performance degrades substantially on ColorMNIST at ρ=99% (56.0%), limiting scalability

Methodological limitations inadequately addressed: (1) Group-wise mean decomposition assumes means capture essential variation—no validation for heterogeneous groups; (2) Method assumes spurious correlations specifically between domain and label, cannot handle other corruption types; (3) Σ-covariance stability from batches during training not analyzed; no ablation on this practical concern

Reproducibility concerns: Code URL is blank despite reproducibility claims. Hyperparameter selection process incomplete (unclear if per-dataset tuning used). Environment inference experiments limited to ColorMNIST with only one noisy setting (Table 14)

Experimental design issues: Group annotations used for model selection across all methods (Table 10), potentially favoring methods designed for group information. ElRep comparison shows variable results suggesting potential dataset-dependence of SCER's advantages

Theoretical robustness fragile: Remark about ±sign in Theorem 1 reveals outcome depends on initialization and training dynamics. Multi-class/multi-domain extensions are empirically validated but not theoretically justified

Missing key analyses: No ablation on why multiply (rather than other combinations) alignment by magnitude; no analysis of convergence properties; limited discussion of failure modes or settings where the spurious-core decomposition breaks down
